title: Founder Mode Is the Wrong Answer to the AI Moment
author: Brian Elliott
summary: Brian Elliott reports on a talk by Dr. Kelly Monahan in which she showed a list of top leadership challenges, skills gaps, tight L&D budgets, young workers who 'don't want to work hard,' technically skilled but unmotivating managers, and revealed it was compiled in the 1950s, using the reveal to argue that AI is exposing organizational design flaws that predate the technology by seven decades rather than creating new ones. Elliott extends Monahan's argument that most 2026 organizations are still running on Taylorism-era architecture: headcount-based reward systems, effort-visibility culture, and rigid org charts, and shows that most current AI 'transformation' is simply headcount reduction with the same processes intact, not genuine redesign of how value gets created. His central target is 'founder mode,' the Paul Graham-derived management philosophy of centralized founder control, which Elliott argues works at ten people, becomes leadership at thirty, and becomes 'cosplay' at thirty thousand, contrasting it with General Stanley McChrystal's Team of Teams model of pushing decisions to where information actually sits, and Barnes & Noble's recovery under James Daunt, who pushed book-buying decisions from headquarters down to individual store managers. The piece closes with data showing a widening trust gap between leadership optimism and workforce skepticism about AI, including Stanford research that 22-to-25-year-olds in AI-exposed occupations now face 19 percent lower employment than less-exposed peers, and three concrete quarterly actions for leaders: delegate one class of decision explicitly, state what's staying the same, and change what gets rewarded.
points: Monahan's list-of-challenges reveal (identical leadership complaints dating to the 1950s) is used to reframe the entire AI-transformation conversation: 'AI is becoming a very expensive way to realize how poorly designed our workplaces were in the first place.'

Elliott's critique of 'founder mode' is scale-specific rather than categorical: centralized founder control is legitimate leadership at 30 people and becomes 'cosplay' at 30,000, directly challenging Paul Graham's widely circulated framework as a permission structure for micromanagement at scale.

The Barnes & Noble case study under James Daunt operationalizes the alternative to founder mode concretely: pushing book-buying decisions from headquarters to individual store managers, resulting in 50 new store openings and a return toward all-time-high performance.

Stanford's Digital Economy Lab data, that 22-to-25-year-olds in AI-exposed occupations face employment 19 percent below less-exposed peers (up from 15 percent a year prior), grounds the piece's trust-gap argument in a specific, worsening labor-market statistic rather than general sentiment.

The reward-system finding that only 13 percent of AI users feel rewarded for reinventing work under short-term performance hits, while 45 percent say it's safer to just hit today's number, identifies the specific incentive misalignment blocking the deeper redesign Elliott argues AI transformation actually requires.
quotes: Kelly's take: "AI is becoming a very expensive way to realize how poorly designed our workplaces were in the first place.
Most reward systems still pay you for the number of humans you manage rather than the outcomes you generate, which is why every reorg turns into a headcount negotiation.

Instead, most AI transformation to date is mostly just cutting: leave the function as-is, reduce by 20% and the survivors have to adopt AI to deliver against the old output goals. No changes to the machine itself, just a different fuel mix.
In a startup of 10 people, you can have a hive mind; as you scale to 30, founder mode is leadership. At thirty thousand, it's cosplay.

James Daunt pushed power out of HQ and gave book buying decisions back to store managers: what to stock, how to shelve it, and what goes on the front table... It worked. The center got smaller, and they opened 50 stores last year, back near their all-time high.
Stanford's Digital Economy Lab finds employment for 22-to-25-year-olds in AI-exposed occupations runs about 19% below the comparison with peers in less-exposed jobs, up from 15% a year ago.

What people are desperate for right now is a sense of steadiness. No matter what's coming at us, this is who I am, this is how I show up every day, and this is the value we're going to create together.
Only 13% of AI users feel rewarded for reinventing work if there's a short term hit and 45% say it's safer to just focus on hitting today's number.
